chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Fazzal, from Ibn Bukayr, and Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from a man, all from Zurara, who said:

Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said to me: 'What do you say about the People of the A'raf?' I said: 'They are nothing but either believers or disbelievers. If they enter Paradise, they are believers, and if they enter the Fire, they are disbelievers.'

He (peace be upon him) said: 'By Allah, they are neither believers nor disbelievers. Had they been believers, they would have entered Paradise just as the believers entered it, and had they been disbelievers, they would have entered the Fire just as the disbelievers entered it. But they are a people whose good deeds and evil deeds are equal, so their deeds fell short, and indeed they are as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said.'

I said: 'Are they from the people of Paradise or from the people of the Fire?' He said: 'Leave them where Allah has left them.' I said: 'So shall I postpone them?' He said: 'Yes, I postpone them just as Allah has postponed them. If He wills, He will admit them to Paradise by His mercy, and if He wills, He will drive them to the Fire because of their sins, and He will not wrong them.'

I said: 'Will a disbeliever enter Paradise?' He said: 'No.' I said: 'Will anyone enter the Fire except a disbeliever?' He said: 'No, except if Allah wills. O Zurara! Indeed, I say 'What Allah wills', and you do not say 'What Allah wills'. Know that when you grow old, you will retract, and your knots will be loosened from you.'
ai.seo_question: Who are the People of the A'raf and what is their fate according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In this narration from al-Kafi, Imam al-Baqir (AS) elucidates the status of the People of the Heights (Ashab al-A'raf) as a distinct intermediate group whose good and evil deeds are perfectly balanced, preventing immediate entry into either Paradise or Hell. The Imam emphasizes their state of 'suspension' (tarjih), where their ultimate fate remains contingent upon Allah's will—either through divine mercy or the weight of their sins—highlighting the balance between justice and grace in Shia eschatology. This discussion underscores the concept of purgatorial waiting, where the barrier of the Heights serves as a temporary abode for those awaiting final judgment.
